text: The London Marathon has three colour-coded starts in Greenwich Park - Blue (elite men + championship), Red (elite women + most Good-for-Age), and Green (remaining runners). All three merge near Woolwich Road by mile 3. Know your start colour and follow signs from your designated assembly area.
label: Runner tactic

text: Baggage buses are located near each start area in Greenwich Park. You must use the official clear bag provided and label it with your runner number. Bags are transported to The Mall finish area and reunited at the designated baggage reunion point on Horse Guards Parade. Expect 20–40 minute waits post-finish.
label: Runner tactic

text: April weather in London averages 8–14°C (46–57°F) with a high chance of rain. Layers are essential at the start - many runners wear disposable bin bags or old charity shop clothes they can discard at the start line. Wind chill along the Thames corridor (especially at Canary Wharf) can feel significantly colder.
label: Runner tactic

text: Aid stations are positioned approximately every mile along the London Marathon course. Water is available from the start; Lucozade Sport is offered from mile 5 onward. Gels (typically Lucozade) are available near miles 14 and 21. Know what your stomach tolerates - do not try new nutrition on race day.
label: Runner tactic

text: The Cutty Sark at mile 6 creates an incredible tunnel of noise - the road narrows around the ship and spectators pack both sides. The energy surge here tempts runners to speed up. Resist. You are not even a quarter done. Bank the adrenaline for miles 20+.
label: Runner tactic

text: Tower Bridge at mile 12–13 has cobblestone sections and metal expansion joints that can be slippery when wet. The bridge is also cambered - slightly higher in the centre. Run the middle for the flattest line and watch your footing, especially in rain.
label: Runner tactic

text: Canary Wharf (miles 17–19) creates a wind tunnel effect between the tall buildings, especially on Westferry Road and around the docklands loop. Headwinds here can sap energy. Tuck behind a group if possible and keep your cadence steady.
label: Runner tactic

text: The Highway (miles 21–23) is where the London Marathon is truly raced. The crowds thin out, the Isle of Dogs loop has taken its toll, and the flat exposed road along the Thames offers little shelter. This is 'The Wall' equivalent. Have a mental strategy prepared - break it into lamp posts, mile markers, or count steps.
label: Runner tactic

text: The finish on The Mall towards Buckingham Palace is the most iconic marathon finish in the world. The final 385 yards are lined with grandstands and the noise is deafening. Lift your head, find your name on the big screen, and enjoy it - you've earned this moment.
label: Runner tactic

text: The first 5km from Greenwich Park is predominantly downhill. This is a trap. Your legs feel fresh and gravity is helping - but every second you bank here will cost you double after mile 20. Start 10–15 seconds per mile slower than goal pace and let the downhill do the work without overstriding.
label: Failure mode

text: The Cutty Sark (mile 6, Greenwich) is the single best spectator spot on the London Marathon course. Arrive by 09:30 to secure a front-row position. The road narrows around the ship creating an amphitheatre effect - the noise is unreal. Take DLR to Cutty Sark station (2 min walk).
label: Spectator tactic

text: Tower Bridge (mile 12–13) is spectacular but extremely crowded for spectators. The bridge itself is closed to spectators during the race - you must watch from the approach roads on either side. The south side (Bermondsey) is slightly less packed than the north side (Tower Hill).
label: Spectator tactic

text: Canary Wharf (miles 17–19) offers good viewing with more space than central spots. The wide roads around the docklands give better sightlines. Use Canary Wharf Jubilee line station - it's the spectator's secret weapon for quick repositioning to Westminster or London Bridge.
label: Spectator tactic

text: The Embankment (miles 24–25) near Blackfriars and Temple is where runners need you most. The race is nearly won or lost here - your cheering genuinely makes a difference. Westminster or Embankment tube stations are closest. Arrive early as the area fills fast.
label: Spectator tactic

text: Crossing the marathon course on foot is nearly impossible once the race begins. The route forms a continuous loop from Greenwich through Deptford, Bermondsey, Tower Bridge, Canary Wharf, The Highway, Embankment, and The Mall. Use the Tube or DLR to get between sides - do NOT attempt surface crossings.
label: Spectator tactic

text: The DLR and Jubilee Line are the spectator lifelines for the London Marathon. DLR connects Greenwich/Cutty Sark to Canary Wharf to Bank (for Tower Bridge area). Jubilee connects Canary Wharf to Westminster (for The Mall finish). Master these two lines and you can see your runner 3 times.
label: Transit strategy

text: Three-View Rule: Attempting more than 3 viewing positions consistently fails for spectators. Transit disruptions, course crossing impossibility, and crowd density make a 4th move nearly impossible for runners slower than 3:15. Recommended trio: Cutty Sark (mile 6) → Canary Wharf (mile 18) → Embankment (mile 25).
label: Spectator tactic

text: Post-finish, runners exit the chute on The Mall, collect their medal, heat sheet, and goodie bag, then proceed to Horse Guards Parade for the reunion area. The walk from finish line to meeting points takes 20–45 minutes due to channelled exit paths, medal collection, and congestion.
label: Runner tactic

text: Reunion without a pre-agreed plan averages 45–90 minutes. Mobile signal near the finish is severely degraded due to 50,000+ spectators around The Mall. Designate a meeting letter zone (A–Z) at Horse Guards Parade as primary and Victoria Station food court as backup.
label: Spectator tactic

text: Numerous bus routes through central, south-east, and east London are diverted or suspended on marathon day from approximately 06:00 to 18:00. Do NOT rely on buses. Use the Tube (Jubilee, District, Northern, Central lines) and DLR exclusively.
label: Transit strategy

text: For the start, runners should take the Southeastern train to Blackheath or Maze Hill stations, or the DLR to Greenwich/Cutty Sark then walk up to Greenwich Park. Dedicated shuttle buses run from certain stations. Allow at least 90 minutes from central London. Gates close 30 minutes before your wave start.
label: Transit strategy

text: Greenwich is ideal for runners wanting a stress-free race morning - walk to the start. London Bridge/Borough and Canary Wharf are also excellent, both within 15–20 minutes by DLR or train. Westminster puts you near the finish but requires a longer journey to Greenwich.
label: Lodging strategy

text: The assembly area in Greenwich Park opens around 07:00 for a 10:00 mass start. There are portaloos (long queues - go early and go often), charity village tents, and warm-up areas. Bring a bin bag to sit on as the grass is often damp. The atmosphere is nervous but electric.
label: Runner tactic

text: Use the London Marathon app or TCS tracking to follow your runner in real time. Timing mats are at 5km intervals, halfway, and the finish. Share your runner's bib number with spectators so they can track independently - do NOT rely on phone calls or texts as mobile networks are congested along the course.
label: Spectator tactic

text: Birdcage Walk into The Mall - the final 800m - is where you will hear the loudest crowd noise on the course. The slight right turn onto The Mall with Buckingham Palace ahead is overwhelming. If you have any energy left, this is where to use it. Arms up, big finish, find the camera.
label: Runner tactic

text: Security screening at Greenwich Park entrance creates a bottleneck between 07:30–09:00. Bag checks are thorough. No large rucksacks permitted - use the official clear bag only. Experienced runners arrive by 07:30 to clear security before the rush.
label: Security reality

text: Portaloo queues in Greenwich Park peak between 08:00–09:15. Veterans arrive by 07:30 and use the toilets immediately. By 08:30, waits of 20–30 minutes are common. Some runners use cafe toilets in Greenwich town before entering the park.
label: Runner tactic

text: The walk from Greenwich Park assembly area to your start pen takes 10–20 minutes depending on your wave. You will be called to move to the start pens approximately 30–45 minutes before your wave. Do NOT leave the portaloo queue too late - missing your wave means starting at the back.
label: Runner tactic

text: Each aid station stretches approximately 200m along the course. Approach from the far end to avoid the initial crowd crush where most runners stop. Water is in bottles (not cups) - grab, squeeze, drink, discard to the side. The road gets slippery with spilled water - shorten your stride through stations.
label: Runner tactic

text: Mile markers are positioned on the left side of the road. Official pace groups wear coloured balloons - 3:00, 3:15, 3:30, 3:45, 4:00, 4:30, 5:00. Locking onto a pace group takes the mental burden off watching your GPS. Find your group in the start pen and stay with them through at least mile 18.
label: Runner tactic

text: Deptford and Rotherhithe (miles 4–8 and 8–11) have some of the best local crowd support. Families set up music, barbecues, and hand out sweets. These communities treat marathon day as a local festival. Don't skip these sections as a spectator - the vibe is amazing and far less crowded than Tower Bridge.
label: Spectator tactic

text: The Isle of Dogs loop (miles 14–21) is mentally the toughest section. You run out along the north side of the docks, loop around, and run back along the south side - seeing runners ahead and behind you at the same time. Break this into three chunks: miles 14–16 (Limehouse), 16–18 (Canary Wharf), 18–21 (return). Celebrate each chunk.
label: Runner tactic

text: Vaseline/anti-chafe is available at some aid stations but do NOT rely on it. Apply your own before the start - nipples, inner thighs, under arms, feet. London Marathon weather can change mid-race (rain then sun) which makes chafing worse. Plasters over nipples are the most reliable prevention.
label: Runner tactic

text: Write your name on the front of your shirt in large letters. London crowds will shout your name for the entire 26.2 miles - the personal encouragement from strangers is one of the most extraordinary things about this marathon. It genuinely helps at miles 20+.
label: Runner tactic

text: Spectators at Tower Bridge often try to cross to the other side via the bridge - this is impossible on race day. The bridge is part of the course and fully closed. If you're on the wrong side, use Tower Hill station (District/Circle) or London Bridge station (Northern/Jubilee) to cross underground.
label: Spectator tactic

text: S-Bahn Ring equivalent: the Jubilee Line runs normally on marathon Sunday and connects the key spectator points - Cutty Sark (via DLR at Canary Wharf), Canary Wharf, London Bridge, Westminster. It runs underground the entire way so surface road closures don't affect it.
label: Transit strategy

text: Bank station is functional but the surface-level exits can dump you on the wrong side of course barriers. The station complex is enormous with long walking tunnels between lines. Use Monument exit for the south (Tower Bridge approach) or Bank exit for the north. Allow 10 extra minutes for navigation.
label: Transit strategy

text: Late arrival to Greenwich Park (after 09:00) triggers a cascade failure: security queue 15+ min, portaloo impossible without missing start pen call, baggage bus rushed. Veterans call this 'the cascade' - one late step ruins every following step. Arrive by 07:30.
label: Failure mode

text: Heat sheets (foil blankets) are distributed immediately after the finish line. Put yours on IMMEDIATELY - your body temperature drops rapidly after stopping. Many runners skip this and regret it within 5 minutes. The heat sheet is not optional; it's medical prevention.
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Body temp drops within ~5 min of stopping

text: Medal engraving is available at the finish area for a fee. Queue times are typically 20–40 minutes during peak finish hours (12:00–15:00). Many runners skip this and order engraving online later through the official London Marathon shop.
label: Runner tactic

text: The London Marathon Expo at the ExCeL Centre (usually Thursday–Saturday before race day) is where you collect your race number, timing chip, and official bag. You MUST attend in person with photo ID - no one else can collect for you. Go on Thursday or Friday morning to avoid Saturday crowds.
label: Runner tactic

text: Charity runners make up a huge proportion of the London Marathon field - over £1 billion raised since 1981. Many charity tents are in Greenwich Park with supporters. If you're running for charity, your tent is a warm, friendly base. Use it for toilets and shelter before the start.
label: Runner tactic

text: Do NOT wear brand new shoes on race day. Your race shoes should have at least 30–50 miles on them. The London Marathon course includes road camber, cobblestones (Tower Bridge), metal grates, and potentially wet surfaces - you need shoes your feet already trust.
label: Runner tactic

text: The crowds along the entire 26.2 miles are what make London special - an estimated 500,000+ spectators line the course. There are very few 'dead zones'. Even The Highway (miles 21–23), the quietest stretch, still has consistent support. London runners consistently say the crowd carries them through the final miles.
label: Runner tactic

text: If spectating near the finish on The Mall, The Mall is closed to the public beyond certain barriers. Arrive at least 60 minutes before your runner's expected finish time. Birdcage Walk (parallel street) offers better access. St James's Park tube station is closer than Westminster for this section.
label: Spectator tactic

text: Make a race-day checklist the night before: bib number pinned to shirt (4 pins, not 2), timing chip on shoe, Vaseline applied, breakfast eaten 3 hours before start, phone charged, meeting plan written on arm in marker, disposable layers packed. Missing any of these causes race-morning panic.
label: Runner tactic

text: London Bridge station exits: if heading to the south side (Bermondsey/Tower Bridge south approach), use the Tooley Street exit. For the north side (Tower Hill/Monument), take the Northern or Jubilee line to Bank/Monument. Getting this wrong wastes 15–20 minutes navigating road closures.
label: Transit strategy

text: Spectator signs with your runner's name are incredibly effective. Make them large, bright, and hold them HIGH above the crowd. Runners are scanning at eye level and above - signs held at waist height are invisible. Use their name, not just 'Go runner!' - personalised signs get spotted.
label: Spectator tactic

text: Post-race protein and carbs within 30 minutes of finishing are crucial for recovery. The goodie bag contains some snacks but bring your own recovery food. A banana + protein bar + electrolyte drink is the minimum. Borough Market (15 min walk from finish) is perfect for a proper post-race meal.
label: Runner tactic

text: The London Marathon course is one of the flattest World Major marathons - total elevation gain is approximately 40m. However, the first 3 miles are noticeably downhill, there are short sharp inclines at the Rotherhithe Tunnel approach (mile 9) and at the Highway overpass (mile 22), and cobblestones at Tower Bridge add difficulty. It is fast but not flat.
label: Runner tactic

text: Your GPS watch will lose accuracy in the Canary Wharf section (miles 17–19) due to tall buildings blocking satellite signals. Pace readings will spike wildly - showing 4:00/mile then 12:00/mile. Switch your watch to LAP PACE instead of current pace, which averages out the noise. Better yet, run by effort and breathing, not your watch, through this section.
sourceName: Coach Magazine - Garmin Watch London Marathon Tips
label: Runner tactic

text: There is a thin blue line painted on the road surface marking the official measured shortest route (the tangents). Following this line means running exactly 26.2 miles. It may be too crowded to follow in the first half, but after mile 16 when the field spreads out, sticking to the blue line can save you 200–400m over the final 10 miles.
label: Runner tactic

text: CRITICAL: Do NOT use Cutty Sark DLR station to get to the start on race morning - it is EXIT ONLY for passengers. You cannot leave the train there. Use Greenwich or Maze Hill stations instead, or take the Southeastern train to Blackheath. This catches people every year.
sourceName: Transport for London / London Marathon Community
label: Transit strategy
timeText: Cutty Sark DLR = EXIT ONLY race morning

text: Runners get FREE travel on race day - show your race bib for free travel on Underground, Overground, DLR, and London buses until 18:30. This also applies to Southeastern trains to the start. Take advantage of this to avoid queuing for tickets on a stressful morning.
label: Transit strategy

text: Dress for mile 3, not the start line. Once you're warmed up (about 15 minutes in), that's where you want to be comfortable. Overdressing is one of the most common race day mistakes - you will overheat by mile 10 and there's no fixing it. Wear a bin bag at the start and discard it.
sourceName: The Runner Beans - London Marathon Tips
label: Runner tactic

text: The portaloos closer to the train stations at Greenwich have the longest queues. Walk further into Greenwich Park toward your start colour zone - the toilets near the actual start pens have significantly shorter queues. Veterans use cafe toilets in Greenwich town BEFORE entering the park.
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Walk deeper into park for shorter queues

text: The three starts merge around mile 2.8 in the middle of a fairly long, steady downhill. This convergence creates congestion - don't panic if you slow down here. Stay patient, keep your rhythm, and don't waste energy weaving. The road opens up significantly after mile 4.
label: Runner tactic

text: Break the race into 5K chunks mentally, not 26.2 miles. Focus only on the next 3.1 miles at a time. Each 5K segment has a different character: 0–5K (downhill start), 5–10K (Cutty Sark energy), 10–15K (Tower Bridge high), 15–20K (Canary Wharf grind), 20–25K (The Highway test), 25–finish (crowd carries you home).
sourceName: Running and the City - Course Strategy
label: Runner tactic

text: There are five official accessible viewing areas for wheelchair users and one carer at: Cutty Sark, Canary Wharf, Butcher Row (The Highway), Tower Hill, and Victoria Embankment. The Highway has dedicated disabled parking at Bishop Challoner School (via Commercial Road) with a level 300m walk to the course.
label: Spectator tactic

text: The Isle of Dogs loop (miles 14–21) lets spectators see runners TWICE from the same spot without moving. Position yourself on the A1261 (Aspen Way) overpass or near Westferry Road and you can see runners going out (mile 15–16) and coming back (mile 19–20). This is the laziest and most effective spectating hack.
label: Spectator tactic
timeText: See runners twice from one spot

text: The meeting area at Horse Guards Parade is organised alphabetically by runner surname - find the letter matching your runner's last name initial. Agree on this IN ADVANCE and write it on your arm. Runners take 15–30 minutes to walk from finish line to Horse Guards. Do not expect them immediately after the app shows they finished.
sourceName: London Marathon Spectator Guide / Community Reports
label: Spectator tactic

text: Nearest tube stations to Horse Guards Parade reunion area: Charing Cross (6 min walk), Embankment (9 min walk), St James's Park (7 min walk), Westminster (10 min walk). Charing Cross is the closest but gets extremely congested. St James's Park is a better option with fewer crowds.
label: Transit strategy
timeText: St James's Park tube = best for reunion

text: If trains to Greenwich are rammed on race morning, consider the Thames Clipper river bus from central London to Greenwich Pier - services run every 20 minutes and the pier is a short walk to the assembly areas. It's often overlooked and far less crowded than the DLR or Southeastern trains.
label: Transit strategy
timeText: River bus every 20 min to Greenwich

text: Organisers warn of up to 90-minute waits to board trains at some stations on race morning. If you're staying in central London, plan to leave by 06:30 at the latest. Those staying in Greenwich should count themselves lucky - walk to the start and save the stress.
label: Transit strategy
timeText: Up to 90-min train waits race morning

text: Southeastern runs extra trains to Greenwich and Maze Hill every 10 minutes from London Bridge starting around 07:00. London Bridge is the key hub station for getting to the start. If you're coming from north London, take the Northern or Jubilee line to London Bridge, then change to Southeastern.
label: Transit strategy
timeText: Trains every 10 min from London Bridge

text: Each start colour has a different nearest station: BLUE start → Blackheath station, GREEN start → Maze Hill station, RED start → Greenwich station. Using the wrong station adds a 15–20 minute walk through the park. Check your start colour on your race number and plan accordingly.
label: Runner tactic

text: The Rotherhithe Tunnel approach around mile 9 has a short sharp incline that surprises many runners. It's the first real uphill on the course. Don't change your effort - just accept the pace will slow slightly for 200m. The crowd support through Surrey Quays and Rotherhithe is excellent to carry you through.
label: Runner tactic

text: After mile 25, Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament come into view. This is the final psychological boost - the finish is less than a mile away. The Victoria Embankment section is ALL flat or slightly downhill. If you have been holding anything back, this is where to spend it. You WILL be carried by the crowd.
sourceName: Running and the City - Course Strategy
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Big Ben = less than 1 mile to go

text: Kerridge's Bar & Grill inside the Corinthia Hotel is right at the finish on The Mall - perfect for a celebratory post-race meal. Book well in advance for marathon Sunday. Alternatively, walk 15 minutes to Borough Market (via Waterloo Bridge) for endless casual food options.
label: Lodging strategy

text: If you bonk or hit the wall (usually miles 18–22), WALK through the next aid station, take on water AND a gel, then start a run/walk pattern: run 4 minutes, walk 1 minute. This is not giving up - it's damage control. Many runners who walk strategically still finish under their target time because walking prevents a complete collapse.
sourceName: The Running Channel - Ultimate London Marathon Guide
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Walk/run = damage control, not giving up

text: The Green Start is located at St John's Park, just off Maze Hill. It's the start for most ballot runners. Your assembly area and baggage buses are separate from the Blue and Red starts, so follow the GREEN signs from your station.
sourceName: World Marathoner - London Marathon Start Area Guide
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start hack: Maze Hill is the recommended station, but the walk from Maze Hill to the Green Start is uphill and can feel draining before you've even started. Consider using Blackheath station instead - it's the same distance but completely flat. Your legs will thank you.
sourceName: Coach Magazine - London Marathon Travel Guide
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Maze Hill or Blackheath: 10-15 min walk

text: Green start baggage buses close 45 minutes before your wave start. Drop your bag early. The walk from the baggage area to your start pen takes another 10-15 minutes, so plan backwards from your wave time: bag drop, final toilet visit, then walk to pen.
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Bag drop closes 45 min before wave

text: Green start toilets: there are portaloos throughout the assembly area, plus Peequal female urinals which often have shorter queues. Use them as soon as you arrive. Once you walk into the start pens there are a few more portaloos, but the queues are much shorter since most people have already gone.
sourceName: The Running Channel - Ultimate London Marathon Guide
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start waves begin at 09:50 (first wave) through to 11:30 (final wave). Check your race number for your exact wave and pen letter. Gates close 30 minutes before each wave, so if your wave is 10:15, you need to be in your pen by 09:45 at the latest.
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start runners merge with Blue start runners around mile 2.8, then all three starts (Green, Blue, Red) are fully merged by mile 3. Expect a pinch point and congestion here. Don't weave or surge - just hold your line and let it sort itself out. The road opens up significantly by mile 4.
sourceName: Coach Magazine - London Marathon Route Guide
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start clothing hack: the wait in the assembly area can be 1-2 hours in April temperatures (8-14C). Bring old clothes, a bin bag poncho, or a cheap charity shop fleece to wear over your race kit. Discard them at the start line - they're collected and donated to charity. Hand warmers in your pockets are a game-changer.
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start charity runners: if you're running for a charity, find your charity tent in the assembly area first. They often have their own portaloos (shorter queues!), warm drinks, and a place to sit. Some charities provide pre-race breakfast. Check with your charity coordinator before race day.
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Charity tents have their own toilets

text: Green start travel timeline: if staying in central London, leave by 06:30. Take the train from London Bridge to Maze Hill or Blackheath (extra services run every 10 min). Arrive by 07:30-08:00. Clear security, use toilets, drop bag, find charity tent if applicable, second toilet visit, walk to pen. Budget 90 min from arrival to pen.
sourceName: Run to the Finish - London Marathon Course Tips
label: Runner tactic
timeText: Budget 90 min from arrival to pen

text: Green start hydration packs and running belts are allowed. You can carry your own water bottle, gels, and nutrition. Many green start runners carry their own supplies for the first half and then rely on course aid stations from mile 13 onward. A small running belt with 4-6 gels and a soft flask is the most popular setup.
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start first mile: the Green Start route runs through St John's Park and onto Charlton Way. It's a fast downhill for the first 2 miles. You'll feel amazing, the crowd is buzzing, and gravity is pulling you along. This is the biggest pacing trap on the course. Trust your training pace, not your excitement.
label: Runner tactic

text: Green start sanitary products: sanitary products, hair ties, breast pads, tissues, and wet wipes are available at all drinks stations, information points, and the start area changing rooms. You don't need to pack these yourself.
label: Runner tactic
